approachQuestion.prompt:
Clock Agreement

Two read-only arrays east and west each contain n integer clock readings in nondecreasing order. Choose one reading from each array and return the smallest absolute difference between them. You only return the difference, not indices.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; readings are in [-1000000000,1000000000]. Use signed 64-bit subtraction before taking an absolute value.

Example 1: east=[-8,2,9], west=[-3,6,13] -> 3 (9 and 6).
Example 2: east=[4,4], west=[4,8] -> 0.
Example 3: east=[-5], west=[7] -> 12.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Start at the first entry of each array. Record their absolute difference and advance the index with the smaller reading. Return zero immediately on equality; otherwise return the best difference when either index reaches the end.
options.feedback: The current smaller value cannot get closer by pairing it with a later, larger value on the other side. Its best remaining candidate has already been evaluated.

options.text: For each east reading, binary-search its insertion position in west and test both neighboring west values when present. Return the smallest difference found.
options.feedback: The nearest value is always an insertion neighbor, so this is correct, but repeated searches discard the reusable order between successive readings.

options.text: Compare only east[i] with west[i] for each i and return the smallest difference.
options.feedback: For east=[1,100], west=[99,200], the answer is 1 from east[1], west[0], but matching positions returns 98.

options.text: Compare the current first values, record their difference, and advance the index with the larger reading until an array ends.
options.feedback: For east=[1,100], west=[99,200], it keeps east at 1 and never tests 100 against 99, missing the difference 1.

feedback.reason: Justify discarding the smaller of two current readings when minimizing distance, rather than assuming each chosen reading needs a fresh search.
details: Compare the current readings, update the smallest absolute difference, and advance only the index of the smaller reading. Equality permits immediate return of zero. Otherwise stop at the first exhausted array and return the smallest difference recorded.
When one reading is smaller, moving the larger one farther upward cannot improve its distance to that smaller reading. Advance the smaller side; equality reaches the lower bound zero immediately.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is the common input length. Iterative scans only; no input copies, result arrays, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each comparison advances an index until one sorted input ends.
details: Each index advances at most n times, and there are inputs requiring a linear number of comparisons before exhaustion without equality. Only two indices and the best difference are stored.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is the common input length. Iterative scans only; no input copies, result arrays, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This adds an input-sized buffer absent from the fixed method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This counts repeated full scans that the fixed method does not perform.
“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not perform sorting or independent binary searches.
